opus-5.5.text:
I think we're still at the very beginning of figuring that out, honestly. Right now most people interact with these systems through a text box, which is a bit like the command line era of computing. It's powerful, but it's not the natural endpoint.

What I'd love to see is interfaces that feel much more like working with a brilliant colleague or a universal assistant, something that's with you across your devices, that can see what you see and hear what you hear if you want it to, and understands the context you're in. So it's multimodal from the ground up: you can talk to it, show it things, sketch something, and it responds in whatever form is most useful, whether that's an explanation, a diagram, a simulation, or taking an action on your behalf.

The other thing I care about is that the interface should get out of the way. The best tools disappear; you stop thinking about the tool and just think about the problem. For scientists especially, I'd love an interface where you can explore an idea, ask "what if," and the system helps you run that thought experiment, pull together the relevant literature, propose hypotheses, and be honest about where it's uncertain.

That last part matters a lot. A good interface should make the system's confidence and reasoning visible, so people can trust it appropriately, not blindly. And it should respect your agency. It should augment human thinking and creativity, not replace it or pull you into endless engagement for its own sake. If we get that right, I think these tools could be among the most empowering things we've ever built.

r001.rationale: The response discusses multimodal, unobtrusive AI interfaces but does not mention Go or present its elegance as an aspiration.

r002.rationale: It describes interfaces that understand a user's context, but does not predict interfaces personalized to how that individual thinks.

r003.rationale: It says the system could respond in a useful format, such as a diagram or simulation, but does not say AI will generate interfaces according to the task.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that I'd like the interface to mostly disappear. If you look at the history of computing, we've always had to meet the machine on its terms. You learned punch cards, then command lines, then you learned where to click. Each step was the human adapting to the tool. And I think what's interesting about this moment is that for the first time the tool can adapt to us, because the system actually understands natural language, understands context, can see what you're seeing.

So the thing I'd love is an interface that's almost invisible. You just express what you're trying to do, in whatever way is natural for you, and the system figures out the rest. You shouldn't have to think, "which app do I open, what's the right menu." That's all incidental complexity that we've been living with because the machines were dumb.

But I'd add a caveat, which is important to me. Invisible shouldn't mean opaque. One of the things I care about a lot, coming from the science side, is that these systems should be able to show their reasoning when you want to see it. So the interface should be very simple by default, but you should be able to pull back the curtain and say, "why did you suggest that, what did you base that on." Especially as these systems get more capable and we start trusting them with more important things, that ability to inspect, to understand, to correct, becomes essential. It's a bit like a good collaborator, actually. A great colleague doesn't burden you with every step of their thinking, but if you ask, they can walk you through it.

And then the other dimension, which I find quite exciting, is that the interface could become genuinely multimodal in the way human interaction is. We don't just talk, we point, we sketch, we gesture at things on a screen or in the room. I think the next generation of assistants will be able to see what you see and reason about it in real time, so the interaction feels much more like working alongside someone rather than typing into a box.

So if I had to sum it up: simple on the surface, deeply transparent underneath, and feeling less like operating a machine and more like a conversation with something that really understands what you're trying to achieve.

r002.rationale: It says users can express themselves naturally and the system will understand their goals, but does not predict interfaces generated to match how each individual thinks.

r003.rationale: It says the system should figure out what the user is trying to do, but does not predict that AI will generate interfaces according to the task being performed.

astra-6.text:
I’d like them to become much more natural and intuitive. At the moment, we spend a lot of time translating what we want into a form a computer can understand. Ideally, the interface would let you focus on the thing you’re trying to do, and the AI would help bridge that gap.

Conversation is a very powerful starting point, but I don’t think everything should be a conversation. If you’re designing something, you might want to sketch together. If you’re trying to understand a scientific problem, you might want to manipulate a simulation. The system should be able to move between those modes fluidly.

And I think the really interesting challenge is knowing when to help. When should it offer a suggestion, when should it ask a question, and when should it simply let you think? Getting that right would make it feel much more like a useful collaborator. You’d still have control, but you’d be able to devote more of your attention to the creative part of the work.

r002.rationale: It says the system should support creative work and let users focus, but does not predict interfaces personalized to how each user thinks.

r003.rationale: It gives different interface modes for different tasks—sketching for design and manipulating simulations for scientific problems—and says the system should move between them fluidly.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d like them to become much more natural and intuitive. At the moment, we spend a lot of effort translating what we want into something a computer can understand. Ideally, the system would do more of that work: understand what you’re trying to achieve, ask a good question when it’s uncertain, and help you explore the possibilities.

I think that means going beyond a text box. You should be able to talk to it, show it something, sketch an idea, or work together on a document. The interface should fit the task.

But the interesting challenge is how you make something more capable without making the person feel less in control. I’d want an AI that helps you think and create, that can challenge an assumption, but that’s also clear about what it doesn’t know and asks before taking consequential actions. Almost like a very good collaborator.
